newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela oil spill impact said limited.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela oil spill impact said limited.

text.p: The environmental impact of an oil spill on Venezuela's coast in northwestern Zulia state was so far limited, according to a leading conservationist who was hopeful on Tuesday no more oil would wash ashore.

Lenin Herrera, president of Instituto de Conservation del Lago Maracaibo (ICLAM), an autonomous group funded by Venezuela's Environment Ministry, said only a tiny proportion of the 60,000 barrel spill had come ashore in Zulia.
Some 17.5 kilometres (10 miles) of coastline in the Gulf of Venezuela had been affected, but only 2.5 kilometres (1.5 miles) was badly harmed.
"Up to now what we are seeing (on the coast) is nothing like the total volume of crude oil," he told Reuters. "Let's just hope that what we can see now is all we're going to see."

The Greek-flagged Nissos Amorgos, carrying 476,000 barrels of heavy Venezuelan crude, ran aground on Friday in a shipping channel at the mouth of Lake Maracaibo, spilling about 25,000 barrels, according to Venezuela's state oil subsidiary Maraven.
The spill grew to 60,000 barrels when the ship was moved for repairs, the Venezuelan Navy said.

ICLAM's Herrera said a strong northeasterly wind on Friday helped push the first spill away from the entrance to Lake Maracaibo out to open sea. "If the slick had flowed into the lake it would have been an ecological disaster," he said, adding that the lake hosts a delicate ecological system with mangroves.

A spokesman for the rescue operation said on Monday night that high winds and swell were hampering attempts to stem the flow of crude, but he did not know if the ship was still leaking oil on Tuesday morning.
The Nissos Amorgos is currently at anchor about 16 miles (25 km) off the west coast of Venezuela's Paraguana peninsula.
